newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Mitterrand tied to wiretaps - reports.
newsitem.headline: France's Mitterrand tied to wiretaps - reports.

text.p: Secret files from Francois Mitterrand's anti-terrorist unit showed the late president personally ordered widespread telephone-tapping now under investigation by magistrates, French media reported on Thursday.
The weekly magazine L'Express and the newspaper Le Monde published what they said were extracts from files seized by DST counter-espionage officers and investigating magistrates in February.

The archives, stored in a garage outside Paris rented by the unit's former head, Christian Prouteau, included recordings of telephone-taps, demands for presidential favours and memos on terrorism suspects.
Both reports said many of the notes destined for Mitterrand carried the president's laconic handwritten comment: "Vu" (Seen).
A scandal over alleged illegal bugging by Mitterrand's office erupted shortly before a 1993 general election in which his Socialist party suffered a landslide defeat.

In a note dated March 16, 1993, days before the election, Prouteau wrote to then-prime minister Pierre Beregovoy: "At no time did I or my staff carry out investigations which had not been requested of us.
"When we suggested them, they were launched only when they had been agreed to by a certain number of aides close to the head of state," the note quoted by both publications said.

Prouteau, two former senior government officials, and three members of the since disbanded unit are under investigation over the alleged telephone tapping of dozens of politicians, writers, lawyers and journalists without judicial permission.

France's supreme court last month rejected a bid to stop the investigation, ruling that the statute of limitations in invasion of privacy cases only applied from the moment the offence was discovered, not the date when it was committed.
Among those whose phones were tapped was actress Carole Bouquet, said to be amorously pursued by a senior presidential aide, jealous of her other admirers.

The former head of Mitterrand's private office, Gilles Menage, has acknowledged the unit carried out wiretapping but said it was strictly for national security purposes. He has demanded official secrets rules be lifted to allow him to defend himself.

However, L'Express said the files made clear a key purpose was to protect Mitterrand's own private life, and in particular the secrecy surrounding his illegitimate daughter, Mazarine, whose existence was only made public in 1994.
One of the main wiretap targets was the late writer Jean-Edern Hallier, who had repeatedly threatened to make public Mazarine's existence.

L'Express quoted a 1984 document in which Prouteau reported to Mitterrand that he had learned from phone tapping that Hallier was due to be the suprise guest on a radio show. He had tipped off another presidential aide who had "done what was necessary" to have the programme cancelled, it said.

Le Monde said the documents also showed that Prouteau had written to Mitterrand expressing concern for his "safety in the broadest sense of the term" when he had to share power for the first time with a hostile conservative government in 1986.
Legal wiretaps can only by approved by magistrates in criminal cases or to protect national security, prevent terrorist threats or safeguard essential scientific or economic information.
